SCAMP: Sparse-Anchor Control Is One Small Projection Pengcheng Fang † † thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: University of Southampton Affiliation: Mogo AI Ltd. Tengjiao Sun 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: University of Southampton Affiliation: Mogo AI Ltd. Xiaoyu Zhan Affiliation: Mogo AI Ltd. Affiliation: Nanjing University Yanwen Guo Affiliation: Nanjing University Hansung Kim Affiliation: University of Southampton Xiaohao Cai Affiliation: University of Southampton Dongjie Fu † † thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Mogo AI Ltd. Abstract Text fixes what a motion is, but not where the body must be. Authoring needs
sparse anchors: chosen joints, at chosen frames, at given positions. Meeting
them currently costs a conditioning branch trained for the task, or hundreds
of per-clip optimisation steps in the architecture’s native variables. In any
generator that decodes a continuous state through a frozen differentiable
decoder, the anchors ask for little and leave most of the state free: a few
hundred numbers against tens of thousands, so the states that meet them form
a set within a few hundred dimensions of the state space itself. Every control
method is a choice inside that set, and the choices differ along the
directions the anchors cannot see and the motion can. Our solver,
SCAMP (sparse-anchor control as a minimum-norm projection), makes the
choice that moves none of them: damped Gauss–Newton in the space of the
anchors, through the frozen decoder alone, training-free, one dimensionless
damping constant. Every increment is a combination of the rows of the anchors’
Jacobian, so the correction is orthogonal to everything they never see, and
the system solved is the request’s size and not the state’s. Applied unchanged
to seven published generators spanning diffusion, token and latent designs, in
anchor error it matches or exceeds every released control method it is
measured against, and closes the anchors on the hosts that ship none. Held to
those rows, a correction can only take the shapes the decoder admits, so its
cost is the decoder’s, and a fixed solver makes that cost measurable: every
generator pays in foot skating, and how much divides by decoder family. A
decoder that spreads a change of state over a window keeps its mean
contact-speed skating within a small multiple of the unconstrained
generator’s own; an analytic recovery displaces the body itself, and skating
multiplies several times over. Our
generator is built to that criterion: a windowed decoder and a sampler trained
through the correction, so it meets its anchors within a shallow solve at
sub-second cost. The decoder’s temporal support is a design criterion for
controllable motion generation. 1 Introduction A foot on a mark, a hand on a door handle, a root passing through a
waypoint: the moment a text-to-motion model meets an authoring task,
the specification stops being a sentence and becomes a small set of
Cartesian constraints on particular joints at particular frames — sparse anchors . Generators meet anchors today with machinery
bought at real expense: a conditioning branch trained for the task,
or per-clip optimisation cast in the architecture’s native variables
— guidance on the
sample ( Karunratanakul et al., 2023 ; Xie et al., 2024 ) , descent on
the initial noise ( Karunratanakul et al., 2024 ) , re-imposition of
observed frames during denoising ( Cohan et al., 2024 ) , descent in
a learned latent space ( Dai et al., 2024 ) . The machinery is out of
proportion to the thing specified: a few hundred scalar constraints,
set against a state of 10 4 10^{4} – 10 5 10^{5} dimensions. The disproportion has a mathematical root. Every one of these mechanisms runs on a generator that produces motion by decoding a continuous state 𝑬 {\bm{E}} — a diffusion sample, a latent, a token model’s code embedding — through a frozen differentiable decoder; call it a host . Under that one shared
assumption, anchor control is a single problem: find the state
nearest the host’s own output whose decoded motion meets the anchors, min 𝑬 ⁡ 1 2 ​ ∥ 𝑬 − 𝑬 0 ∥ 2 subject to 𝒓 ⁡ ( 𝑬 ) = 𝟎 , \min_{{\bm{E}}}\ \tfrac{1}{2}\,\lVert{\bm{E}}-{\bm{E}}_{0}\rVert^{2}\quad\text{subject to}\quad{\bm{r}}({\bm{E}})=\bm{0}, (1) where 𝑬 0 {\bm{E}}_{0} is the host’s own sample and 𝒓 {\bm{r}} stacks the anchor
deviations of the decoded motion. What that problem asks is small; what it leaves open is not. Write 𝑱 {\bm{J}} for
the Jacobian of 𝒓 {\bm{r}} : one row per anchor coordinate, m m of them, against one
column per coordinate of the state, P P of those — a few hundred against
tens of thousands. The states that meet the anchors therefore form a set of
dimension P − m P-m , and every control method, a trained branch or a guidance
path or re-imposed frames or a latent descent, is a choice inside it. The
choices are not interchangeable: the anchors are blind to those directions and
the motion is not. SCAMP takes the one that moves none of them.
Each accepted increment is a combination of the rows of 𝑱 {\bm{J}} , so it is
orthogonal to ker ⁡ 𝑱 \ker{\bm{J}} , and the correction as a whole is orthogonal to every direction that
stayed invisible to the anchors along the way — five accepted steps enter at
most 5 ​ m 5m of the state’s directions and leave the rest where the generator put
them. Making that choice costs one linear solve. The objective of
problem 1 is exactly quadratic and only the constraint
is linearised, which gives a step of the residual’s own dimension, taken
through the decoder rather than the sampler. The solver, SCAMP, is
damped Gauss–Newton with a single damping constant made dimensionless by the
Jacobian’s own scale, and the system it solves is m × m m\times m on every host:
the request sets its size, not the state. Applied unchanged to seven published hosts it matches or exceeds each released control method in anchor error, without training and, on MDM, MaskControl and OmniControl, in a fraction of its time (§ 4.1 ). Because the correction lives in those rows, the shapes it can take are the
decoder’s and so is what they cost. Every representation
admits the correction, and every one pays for it in foot skating on the way.
The size of the correction fails to predict the cost: the host that
moves the motion farthest pays a fraction of what the host that moves it least pays. What
tracks it is the decoder’s temporal support, the number of frames
that feel a change of one state coordinate. A decoder that reconstructs each frame from a window of state answers an anchor with a local deformation; an analytic recovery moves the body itself, either within the anchored frames or, when the root is integrated, as a velocity bias across the whole prefix. Grouped by decoder family the hosts separate without overlap,
and an intervention inside a single host moves the cost in whichever
direction its decoder leaves open: widening the update’s temporal
basis lowers it on a frame-local decoder and buys nothing on a
windowed one (§ 4.2 ). The finding motivates a windowed decoder. We keep one and build the sampler around it: a
continuous-time Markov chain over motion tokens, conditioned on the
anchor residual and trained through the terminal correction
(§ 3.6 ). It meets its anchors at sub-second cost. Contributions. (i) One operator for anchor
control. Damped Gauss–Newton in the space of the anchors, through the frozen
decoder alone, taking the increment that moves nothing the anchors cannot see
and solving m × m m\times m whatever the size of the state — training-free, one
dimensionless damping constant, tuned per host nowhere. Retrofitted unchanged
onto seven published generators, it matches or exceeds in anchor error the
released control method of every host that ships one, and closes the anchors
on the two that ship none
(§ 4.1 ). (ii) The cost of a correction, read as a
property of the representation. One fixed operator makes the generator the
experimental variable, and the physical cost divides by decoder family, with
the decoder’s temporal support a causal factor in it: the families separate
without overlap in jerk and in mean contact speed (§ 4.2 ). (iii) A generator built to that criterion. A codebook-geometric continuous-time Markov chain over motion tokens,
keeping a windowed decoder and trained through the correction itself,
reaching 0.083 0.083 m anchor error at FID 0.102 0.102 in 0.50 0.50 s per clip
(§ 4.3 ). 2 Related work Control native to motion generators. GMD ( Karunratanakul et al., 2023 ) and
OmniControl ( Xie et al., 2024 ) add a classifier-style gradient
to the denoising steps of a raw-motion diffusion model; the gradient
is evaluated through the decoder’s map to joint positions, which is
equation 4 up to a step size in its large- μ \mu limit.
DNO ( Karunratanakul et al., 2024 ) and
MotionLCM’s CLT ( Dai et al., 2024 ) instead treat the initial
noise or the latent as the decision variable and run hundreds of Adam
steps through the whole sampler; our correction backpropagates
through the decoder alone, never through the sampler. On the trained
side, CondMDI ( Cohan et al., 2024 ) learns a keyframe-conditioned
model and imputes observed frames during sampling, and
MaskControl ( Pinyoanuntapong et al., 2025 ) trains a control
branch on a masked token model with token-space logit optimisation on
top — the strongest prior method in our comparison. Imputation is
our undamped limit: at μ → 0 \mu\to 0 with a time-selection Jacobian,
whose rows are orthonormal, equation 4 is the exact
projection onto the anchors — the most concentrated correction
available, and § 4.2 measures what that concentration
costs. Inverse problems inside a frozen prior. Outside motion this is a developed literature.
RePaint ( Lugmayr et al., 2022 ) resamples observed regions;
manifold-constrained gradients ( Chung et al., 2022 ) , posterior
sampling ( Chung et al., 2023 ) and pseudo-inverse
guidance ( Song et al., 2023 ) steer each denoising step toward the
measurement; the null-space decomposition ( Wang et al., 2023 ) projects each iterate onto the measurement set — for a linear
decoder, the μ → 0 \mu\!\to\!0 limit of our own update;
universal ( Bansal et al., 2024 ) and energy ( Yu et al., 2023 ) guidance backpropagate an arbitrary objective through the denoiser.
Our operator belongs to this family, carried from gradient steps to
damped Gauss–Newton steps and to a general host state. We use it as
an instrument : one solver unchanged across hosts makes the
representation the variable (§ 4.2 ). Differentiable-optimisation
layers ( Amos and Kolter, 2017 ; Pineda et al., 2022 ) supply the machinery
for training through such a solve, as § 3.6 does. Classical constrained motion editing. Spacetime constraints ( Witkin and Kass, 1988 ; Gleicher, 1997 ) and style-based IK ( Grochow et al., 2004 ) solve the same
projection, but against hand-designed regularisers rather than a
learned prior. Here the regulariser is the host’s own decoder, whose
temporal coupling applies to every iterate, and § 4.2 measures how far it reaches. 3 Method Figure 1: The anchors enter twice: during sampling as a feedback signal, the
current clean posterior soft-decoded to joints 𝒑 ^ \hat{{\bm{p}}} and the model
conditioned on 𝑹 = 𝑴 ⊙ ( 𝒀 − 𝒑 ^ ) {\bm{R}}={\bm{M}}\odot({\bm{Y}}-\hat{{\bm{p}}}) through extra keys and values;
at the end as the target of one damped Gauss–Newton solve through the frozen
decoder. The tokeniser is frozen throughout and its decoder is windowed, so a
correction spreads over its receptive field. 3.1 The problem, and what a host must expose The layer consumes two objects: a continuous state 𝑬 ∈ ℝ P {\bm{E}}\in\mathbb{R}^{P} the
generator produces, and a frozen differentiable map 𝒟 \mathcal{D} from
that state to Cartesian joint positions. Any generator supplying them
is a host — 𝑬 {\bm{E}} is a diffusion sample, a latent, or a token
model’s continuous code embedding, and 𝒟 \mathcal{D} composes the
host’s learned decoder, where it has one, with the analytic recovery
of joint positions from its motion representation. On token hosts we decode the corrected state directly, so the correction reaches the motion in full rather than being rounded back onto the codebook. A control request is a set of A A anchors { ( τ a , j a , 𝒚 a ) } \{(\tau_{a},j_{a},{\bm{y}}_{a})\} :
joint j a j_{a} at position 𝒚 a {\bm{y}}_{a} in frame τ a \tau_{a} . Stacking the
deviations gives the residual 𝒓 ⁡ ( 𝑬 ) = [ 𝒟 ⁡ ( 𝑬 ) ​ [ τ a , j a ] − 𝒚 a ] a = 1 A ∈ ℝ m , m = 3 ​ A , {\bm{r}}({\bm{E}})=\left[\,\mathcal{D}({\bm{E}})[\tau_{a},j_{a}]-{\bm{y}}_{a}\,\right]_{a=1}^{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m},\qquad m=3A, (2) and the request specifies problem 1 : the state nearest the host’s own output that zeros 𝒓 {\bm{r}} . Anchors are sparse, so m m is orders of
magnitude below P P . 3.2 The damped Gauss–Newton step Write 𝑱 = ∂ 𝒓 / ∂ 𝑬 ∈ ℝ m × P {\bm{J}}=\partial{\bm{r}}/\partial{\bm{E}}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times P} . Linearising the
constraint of problem 1 at 𝑬 0 {\bm{E}}_{0} gives its
first step: the smallest increment that meets the linearised anchors, min 𝚫 ⁡ 1 2 ​ ∥ 𝚫 ∥ 2 2 subject to 𝑱 ​ 𝚫 = − 𝒓 . \min_{{\bm{\Delta}}}\ \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert{\bm{\Delta}}\rVert_{2}^{2}\quad\text{subject to}\quad{\bm{J}}{\bm{\Delta}}=-{\bm{r}}. (3) Stationarity gives 𝚫 = 𝑱 ⊤ ​ 𝒗 {\bm{\Delta}}={\bm{J}}^{\top}{\bm{v}} with 𝑱 ​ 𝑱 ⊤ ​ 𝒗 = − 𝒓 {\bm{J}}{\bm{J}}^{\top}{\bm{v}}=-{\bm{r}} : the increment lies in the row space of 𝑱 {\bm{J}} ,
and the unknown is the multiplier 𝒗 {\bm{v}} , one coordinate per anchor
coordinate. That row space is the whole of what the anchors can reach: 𝑱 {\bm{J}} has m m rows against P P columns, so its kernel has dimension P − m P-m , and the
increment is orthogonal to all of it, ⟨ 𝚫 , 𝒏 ⟩ = 𝒗 ⊤ ​ 𝑱 ​ 𝒏 = 0 \langle{\bm{\Delta}},{\bm{n}}\rangle={\bm{v}}^{\top}{\bm{J}}{\bm{n}}=0 for every 𝒏 ∈ ker ⁡ 𝑱 {\bm{n}}\in\ker{\bm{J}} . Confining the increment to a trust region, equivalently
relaxing the equality to a quadratic penalty, adds a multiple of the
identity to that system ( Moré, 1978 ) , 𝚫 = − 𝑱 ⊤ ​ ( 𝑱 ​ 𝑱 ⊤ + μ ​ 𝑰 m ) − 1 ​ 𝒓 \boxed{\;{\bm{\Delta}}=-\,{\bm{J}}^{\top}\bigl({\bm{J}}{\bm{J}}^{\top}+\mu{\bm{I}}_{m}\bigr)^{-1}{\bm{r}}\;} (4) which leaves the increment in the row space and so leaves the orthogonality
where it was, and keeps the linear system at m × m m\times m : the request sets its
size, not the state, m = 144 m{=}144 at the anchor density of § 4 against P P in the tens of thousands. The matrix inverted, 𝑱 ​ 𝑱 ⊤ + μ ​ 𝑰 m {\bm{J}}{\bm{J}}^{\top}+\mu{\bm{I}}_{m} , is positive semidefinite by construction and
positive definite for every μ > 0 \mu>0 , so a step exists for any request on any
host. The same increment written in the state, − ( 𝑱 ⊤ ​ 𝑱 + μ ​ 𝑰 P ) − 1 ​ 𝑱 ⊤ ​ 𝒓 -({\bm{J}}^{\top}{\bm{J}}+\mu{\bm{I}}_{P})^{-1}{\bm{J}}^{\top}{\bm{r}} , asks for a P × P P\times P inverse;
only one of the two is computable at this size. A
correction of R R accepted steps therefore enters at most R ​ m Rm of the state’s
directions and leaves the rest of the state exactly where the host put it.
The iteration repeats this step from the corrected state and returns the endpoint of that path; how far it moves the decoded motion is measured per host (Displ. in Table 2 ). At μ → 0 \mu\to 0 and full row rank each step
is the minimum-norm increment of equation 3 — the
property § 3.5 uses — and applied to Cartesian joint
targets equation 4 is the damped least-squares step of
singularity-robust inverse
kinematics ( Wampler, 1986 ; Nakamura and Hanafusa, 1986 ; Chiaverini et al., 1994 ) ,
whose undamped min-norm form goes back
to Ben-Israel (1966) . What differs from that setting is the shape of 𝑱 {\bm{J}} . In inverse kinematics it is analytic and the unknowns are a few dozen
joint angles, so the system can be square or overdetermined and the damping
carries it through kinematic singularities. Here it is read from the frozen
decoder by m m reverse-mode products, and sparse anchors against a generator’s
state make m ≪ P m\ll P by construction: the system is always the underdetermined
one, and the damping is the trust region the linearisation asks for. The loop. We iterate: build 𝑱 {\bm{J}} , solve
equation 4 , and accept the trial only if it strictly
decreases the merit Φ ⁡ ( 𝑬 ) = ∥ 𝒓 ⁡ ( 𝑬 ) ∥ 2 2 \Phi({\bm{E}})=\lVert{\bm{r}}({\bm{E}})\rVert_{2}^{2} . A rejected
trial raises the damping and re-solves the same system; acceptance
lowers it. When every trial at a state is rejected, the solve returns
the last accepted state (constants in Appendix A ). As μ \mu grows the step approaches − 𝑱 ⊤ 𝒓 / μ -{\bm{J}}^{\top}{\bm{r}}/\mu , a descent
direction for Φ \Phi , so a large enough damping yields an accepted
step at any non-stationary state. Solve depth — the number of accepted steps — is chosen per
request at inference and sets the precision. 3.3 Scale-normalised damping One dimensionless constant has to serve hosts whose states differ in
scale by orders of magnitude: a code embedding, a VAE latent and a
normalised motion feature give Gram matrices whose diagonals are not
comparable. We set μ = λ ⋅ 1 m ​ tr ⁡ ( 𝑱 ​ 𝑱 ⊤ ) , \mu\;=\;\lambda\cdot\frac{1}{m}\operatorname{tr}\!\left({\bm{J}}{\bm{J}}^{\top}\right), (5) which makes λ \lambda dimensionless: under 𝑬 ↦ α ​ 𝑬 {\bm{E}}\mapsto\alpha{\bm{E}} we
have 𝑱 ↦ 𝑱 / α {\bm{J}}\mapsto{\bm{J}}/\alpha , so μ ↦ μ / α 2 \mu\mapsto\mu/\alpha^{2} and 𝚫 ↦ α ​ 𝚫 {\bm{\Delta}}\mapsto\alpha{\bm{\Delta}} — the iterate is exactly equivariant,
and rescaling 𝒓 {\bm{r}} leaves it unchanged. A single dimensionless λ 0 = 10 − 2 \lambda_{0}=10^{-2} , set once, initialises the
loop on every host in this paper. Scalar damping is
Levenberg’s ( Levenberg, 1944 ) ; the accept-and-retry
schedule and the curvature-derived scale are
Marquardt’s ( Marquardt, 1963 ) , whose scaling is
per-coordinate where equation 5 is a single scalar;
the trust-region reading and adaptive scaling are Moré (1978) ’s. 3.4 Metric and reparameterisation Solving equation 3 for a reparameterised increment 𝚫 = 𝑩 ​ 𝜶 {\bm{\Delta}}={\bm{B}}{\bm{\alpha}} of smallest ∥ 𝜶 ∥ \lVert{\bm{\alpha}}\rVert gives 𝚫 = − 𝚺 ​ 𝑱 ⊤ ​ ( 𝑱 ​ 𝚺 ​ 𝑱 ⊤ + μ ​ 𝑰 ) − 1 ​ 𝒓 {\bm{\Delta}}=-{\bm{\Sigma}}{\bm{J}}^{\top}({\bm{J}}{\bm{\Sigma}}{\bm{J}}^{\top}+\mu{\bm{I}})^{-1}{\bm{r}} with 𝚺 = 𝑩 ​ 𝑩 ⊤ ⪰ 0 {\bm{\Sigma}}={\bm{B}}{\bm{B}}^{\top}\succeq 0 , a preconditioner: a rectangular 𝑩 {\bm{B}} confines the increment to the subspace its columns span. The damping
scale follows it, μ = λ ​ tr ⁡ ( 𝑱 ​ 𝚺 ​ 𝑱 ⊤ ) / m \mu=\lambda\operatorname{tr}({\bm{J}}{\bm{\Sigma}}{\bm{J}}^{\top})/m , so a change of 𝑩 {\bm{B}} leaves the effective regularisation where it was. We take 𝑩 = 𝑰 {\bm{B}}={\bm{I}} , and so 𝚺 = 𝑰 {\bm{\Sigma}}={\bm{I}} , on the evidence of
Appendix B , except in the intervention of

columns of 𝑩 {\bm{B}} are temporally smooth atoms of controlled width and
widening them restricts the increment to smoother shapes. 3.5 What the state costs: temporal support For every damping the increment lies in the row space of 𝑱 {\bm{J}} . Write 𝑱 = 𝑺 ​ 𝑮 {\bm{J}}={\bm{S}}{\bm{G}} for the decoder’s full Jacobian 𝑮 {\bm{G}} and the selection 𝑺 {\bm{S}} that reads the anchored coordinates: the decoded displacement is
then a combination of the columns of 𝑮 ​ 𝑮 ⊤ ​ 𝑺 ⊤ {\bm{G}}{\bm{G}}^{\top}{\bm{S}}^{\top} , rows
of the decoder’s own Gram, which for a convolutional decoder is the
autocorrelation of its temporal response and so reaches about twice as
far. The host fixes the family of shapes a correction can take; the
request selects which of them, and how much. This width is a property of the frozen map 𝒟 \mathcal{D} alone, and is measured
without a solve: perturb one coordinate of the state at one frame,
decode, and read how far in time the displacement extends. We report
it as w eff = ∑ t d t / max t ⁡ d t w_{\text{eff}}=\sum_{t}d_{t}/\max_{t}d_{t} for d t d_{t} the joint
displacement at frame t t : one for a strictly frame-local decode, growing with the spread. Coordinates are drawn uniformly and the median reported, so it reports the reach of a typical coordinate; the few integrated root channels of an analytic recovery reach further, and § 4.2 reads them in the displacement they produce. The families differ in kind. A learned decoder of temporal receptive
field w w answers an anchor with a deformation supported on a window
— a shape the prior already produces, since the decoder was fitted
to plausible motion. An analytic recovery has no such window. From
absolute-root features it is frame-local in every channel, so the
increment stays inside the anchored frames. From relative-root
features the root is integrated, so the row of an anchor at frame τ \tau is constant over the whole preceding interval and the
minimum-norm increment is a velocity bias of size ∥ 𝒓 ∥ / τ \lVert{\bm{r}}\rVert/\tau applied to every frame up to τ \tau : the body
is displaced, gently but continuously, for the whole prefix. The cost is measured as foot skating, the standard
physical-plausibility artefact of motion synthesis: a foot within 5 5 cm of the ground that moves horizontally faster than 0.5 0.5 m/s,
over a five-frame window at 20 20 fps, counts against the
clip ( Xie et al., 2024 ) . Two things decide the count, the speed each frame carries and
how many contact frames carry it, and the three correction shapes sit
differently on both. A windowed deformation is compact and spread over the decoder’s
window, so the speed it adds at any one contact frame is small. A frame-local correction puts a whole displacement between
two frames, far above the threshold. A root bias is small per frame
and applies to the entire body, so every foot planted anywhere in the
prefix is dragged with it. 3.6 A generator built to the criterion We address the shape by keeping a frozen VQ tokeniser of the MoMask
family ( Guo et al., 2024 ) , whose convolutional decoder is a windowed decode, so a correction is spread over its receptive field; ours uses a single quantiser at unit temporal stride, so
one token corresponds to one frame. We address the magnitude by
conditioning the sampler on the anchor residual and training it through the terminal solve. The
sampler is a continuous-time Markov chain over the token sequence,
whose rates admit only jumps toward the sampled endpoint: an
intermediate sequence stays on the codebook’s local geometry and
decodes to a nearby motion, so the anchor residual is informative from the
first steps and the training gradient reaches the emitted state through it. Codebook-geometric CTMC. We formulate generation as
continuous-time discrete diffusion over the token
sequence ( Austin et al., 2021 ; Campbell et al., 2022 ) and instantiate its
endpoint-conditioned path ( Campbell et al., 2024 ; Gat et al., 2024 ) with the geometry of the frozen token embedding table. We adopt the prototype distance of Fang et al. (2026) : for normalised prototypes 𝒄 ¯ v \bar{{\bm{c}}}_{v} , δ ⁡ ( i , j ) = ∥ 𝒄 ¯ i − 𝒄 ¯ j ∥ 2 2 ​ p \delta(i,j)=\lVert\bar{{\bm{c}}}_{i}-\bar{{\bm{c}}}_{j}\rVert_{2}^{2p} , whose exponent p p sets how sharply the rates concentrate on near neighbours. With an increasing

their positionwise product realises the corresponding product path
over sequences. Proposition 1 is what makes the training corruption and
the sampling dynamics the same process: the prior is trained by
corrupting with q t ( ⋅ ∣ z ⋆ ) q_{t}(\cdot\mid z^{\star}) and predicting z ⋆ z^{\star} , and
the sampler then integrates the generator that path induces. A masked transformer predicts, at each grid time, a clean-token

equation 7 under this posterior gives the controlled
rate, which we realise with one hard endpoint sample per position.

first event gives the parallel kernel P n , ℓ next ​ ( k ) = { exp ⁡ [ − h n ​ H n , ℓ ] , k = i , ( 1 − exp ⁡ [ − h n ​ H n , ℓ ] ) ​ u n , ℓ ​ ( k ) / H n , ℓ , k ≠ i , P^{\mathrm{next}}_{n,\ell}(k)=\begin{cases}\exp[-h_{n}H_{n,\ell}],&k=i,\\[2.84526pt]

the absorbed case. Proposition 2 (Tau-leap consistency) . The product of equation 8 over positions agrees with
the posterior-averaged joint generator to first order in h n h_{n} , with
remainder bounded by C ​ h n 2 ​ 𝔼 ​ [ ℋ n 2 ] Ch_{n}^{2}\,\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{H}_{n}^{2}] for ℋ n = ∑ ℓ H n , ℓ \mathcal{H}_{n}=\sum_{\ell}H_{n,\ell} . The generator the bound refers to is the controlled one, whose clean
posterior guidance and truncation tilt. Its remainder grows with the

the kernel behaves as a small-step integrator through the interior of
the grid and as a commitment to the sampled endpoint at the last
steps. Proofs are in Appendix G . Anchor conditioning. The model sees anchors as a
state-dependent residual: at each step the current clean posterior is
soft-decoded to joint positions 𝒑 ^ \hat{{\bm{p}}} , and the masked residual 𝑹 𝒜 = 𝑴 ⊙ ( 𝒀 − 𝒑 ^ ) {\bm{R}}_{\mathcal{A}}={\bm{M}}\odot({\bm{Y}}-\hat{{\bm{p}}}) — targets 𝒀 {\bm{Y}} , binary
observation mask 𝑴 {\bm{M}} — is concatenated per frame with 𝒀 {\bm{Y}} and 𝑴 {\bm{M}} ,
encoded by a temporal convolutional network, and injected through zero-initialised
low-rank adapters as additional keys and values in every attention block. The
conditioning is a feedback signal on the error of the model’s own current
clean prediction. Solver-coupled training. The VQ encoder, decoder, codebook
and text encoder stay frozen throughout. Training runs in three
stages: a text-conditioned prior trained with clean-token
cross-entropy over the path of equation 6 ; control fine-tuning under the
conditioning above, over a ladder of anchor densities with first and last
frames always observed; and a short on-policy calibration in which the model
generates with its own sampler while the terminal solve sits inside the
training graph. There the sampled prefix carries no graph, the last few states
stay differentiable through hard-forward
transitions ( Jang et al., 2017 ; Maddison et al., 2017 ) , and the solved state
re-enters the loss through the identity surrogate 𝑬 ST = 𝑬 diff + sg ⁡ [ 𝑬 num − 𝑬 diff ] , {\bm{E}}^{\mathrm{ST}}={\bm{E}}^{\mathrm{diff}}+\operatorname{sg}\!\left[{\bm{E}}^{\mathrm{num}}-{\bm{E}}^{\mathrm{diff}}\right], (9) whose forward value is the exact numerical solve and whose Jacobian is
the identity. Differentiating through equation 4 at frozen 𝑱 {\bm{J}} gives 𝑰 − 𝑱 ⊤ ​ ( 𝑱 ​ 𝑱 ⊤ + μ ​ 𝑰 ) − 1 ​ 𝑱 {\bm{I}}-{\bm{J}}^{\top}({\bm{J}}{\bm{J}}^{\top}+\mu{\bm{I}})^{-1}{\bm{J}} , which tends to the
orthogonal projector onto ker ⁡ 𝑱 \ker{\bm{J}} , so the exact path would annihilate
precisely the gradient component along the correction just applied —
the component that reports how far the emitted state was from meeting
the anchors. The anchors act twice and the solver once: they condition every sampler
step, and at the last one the terminal clean state is handed to equation 4 for R = 2 R{=}2 accepted steps under the identity metric, after which the corrected
continuous state is decoded as it stands and never re-quantised
(Algorithm 1 ). What the state it emits then costs to correct is

At matched anchor error the quality cost follows the decoder family as the physical cost does; our generator closes its anchors at FID 0.078 0.078 in 0.50 0.50 s, below MaskControl’s and MotionLCM’s released methods (Appendix F , Table 7 ). The last row is our own generator under the same operator: it emits 0.083 0.083 m and three accepted steps take it to 0.0091 0.0091 m. One damping constant covers all eight,
which rests on the scale normalisation of § 3.3 (Appendix A ). 4.2 Where the physical cost comes from Jerk at the anchored frames measures the mechanism directly, and it
separates the windowed decodes from the analytic recoveries without
overlap (Table 2 ): 21 21 – 52 × 52\times against 1.1 1.1 – 4.6 × 4.6\times , and MARDM at 0.0003 0.0003 m pays a fifth of what MDM pays at 0.0096 0.0096 m. The measured temporal support divides them the same
way, an order of magnitude apart: 1.0 1.0 frame on the analytic recoveries, 28.7 28.7 to 54.2 54.2 on the learned decoders. CondMDI sits where § 3.5 places the sharp limit:
absolute-root and frame-local, its displacement confined to
the anchored frames in every clip, and it pays the most. MDM and OmniControl integrate the root, so on their root channels the correction is a prefix velocity bias — a rigid drift, not a deformation — which moves the body 0.672 0.672 and 0.575 0.575 m, and they still pay 21 21 – 28 × 28\times . Down-weighting those channels in the solver’s metric leaves the cost where it is (Appendix B ). The size of the correction runs the other way from its cost:
MotionLCM moves the motion 0.863 0.863 m and MARDM 0.747 0.747 m, the two
largest displacements measured, at jerk ratios of 2.4 2.4 and 4.6 4.6 ,
while CondMDI moves it 0.039 0.039 m at 51.9 51.9 , the highest. The downstream cost in foot skating depends on which convention
measures it, and the dependence is the mechanism again. Under mean
foot speed during contact the families separate as jerk does, 4.84 4.84 – 6.21 × 6.21\times against 1.12 1.12 – 2.74 × 2.74\times ; under the fraction
of contact frames above the threshold they do not, CondMDI falling to 1.84 × 1.84\times and MARDM rising to 4.67 × 4.67\times : a correction confined to the
anchored frames makes a few very fast slides, which a mean registers and a
count barely does, and one across the clip makes many slow ones. At matched accuracy our generator closes its anchors to 0.0091 0.0091 m
and pays 1.12 × 1.12\times at w eff = 43.1 w_{\text{eff}}{=}43.1 against its deployed output and 1.37 × 1.37\times against its raw sampler output; the separation holds on absolutes as on ratios (Appendix F ). Reparameterising the update through a temporal basis of width w w tests the same variable causally, at fixed weights, decoder, anchors
and solver (Table 6 , Appendix D ). Where the decoder is
frame-local the basis supplies that support from outside and the
physical cost falls monotonically with it, skating 3.87 3.87 to 3.15 × 3.15\times on MDM and 5.40 5.40 to 4.30 × 4.30\times on OmniControl from w = 1 w{=}1 to 8 8 , read at the first depth under a centimetre ( n = 128 n{=}128 ); at w = 16 w{=}16 neither host gets there. On MoMask,
whose decoder already carries w eff = 49.6 w_{\text{eff}}{=}49.6 , the basis buys
nothing: the high-frequency share stays at 0.009 0.009 – 0.011 0.011 , skating
at a centimetre at 1.6 1.6 – 1.8 × 1.8\times over w = 1 w{=}1 to 4 4 , and accuracy
falls, 2.1 × 2.1\times and 3.4 × 3.4\times at depth three for w = 8 w{=}8 and 16 16 ,
neither reaching a centimetre. An explicit basis supplies a smoothness
the windowed decoder already has, and pays for it in the directions
the solve had. 4.3 Our generator Figure 2: Four requests under the six-point protocol, K = 8 K{=}8 . Spheres

The upper block places the generator
before the solve: the prior scores FID 0.043 0.043 at Top-3 0.827 0.827 . Figure 2 shows what those two steps do: the sampler
places the body 0.067 0.067 – 0.836 0.836 m from the anchors and the solve
brings it to 0.008 0.008 – 0.064 0.064 m, closing the largest gap by 17 × 17\times . Trained with R = 1 R{=}1 instead of R = 2 R{=}2 , the same recipe deploys to 0.166 0.166 and 0.087 0.087 m at the two inference depths against the deployed
checkpoint’s 0.165 0.165 and 0.083 0.083 (validation, n = 1024 n{=}1024 ): the second step
buys what a step of the solver buys. Trained post hoc instead, with no solver in its sampler, the same model emits 0.367 0.367 m against 0.314 0.314 and stands at 0.107 0.107 m after the same two steps (Appendix H ). 5 Conclusion Sparse anchors fix a few hundred directions of a state with tens of thousands;
what they leave open is the rest. A training-free damped Gauss–Newton solve of
the anchor residual, one dimensionless damping constant and no per-host tuning,
takes the increment that moves none of it, and in anchor error it matches or
exceeds every released control method it is measured against. What a correction may then look like is the decoder’s to decide, and holding
the solver fixed measures what its shapes cost: at matched anchor accuracy the
decoder families separate without overlap in jerk and in mean contact speed.
Built to that criterion, our generator reaches 0.083 0.083 m at FID 0.102 0.102 .
Temporal support is measurable in advance on any host that exposes a differentiable decode, and is a design choice. Ethics statement This work synthesises human motion from text and Cartesian anchors on
public HumanML3D data, and releases no new human data. The generators
it retrofits are public released checkpoints, used under their own
licences. Reproducibility statement The solver is equation 4 with the schedule and constants
of Appendix A ; the protocol, conformance gate and
metric conventions are in Appendix F ; the generator’s
three training stages are in Appendix H . Code, the
gate’s output and the per-sample records will accompany the paper. Appendix A Solver details The loop, in full. At outer step k k the solver holds a
state 𝑬 k {\bm{E}}_{k} , evaluates 𝒓 k = 𝒓 ⁡ ( 𝑬 k ) {\bm{r}}_{k}={\bm{r}}({\bm{E}}_{k}) and builds 𝑱 k {\bm{J}}_{k} by m m reverse-mode products through 𝒟 \mathcal{D} . A trial
uses μ k = λ k ​ 1 m ​ tr ⁡ ( 𝑱 k ​ 𝑱 k ⊤ ) \mu_{k}=\lambda_{k}\,\tfrac{1}{m}\operatorname{tr}({\bm{J}}_{k}{\bm{J}}_{k}^{\top}) in
equation 4 , and is accepted when Φ ⁡ ( 𝑬 k + 𝚫 ) < Φ ⁡ ( 𝑬 k ) \Phi({\bm{E}}_{k}+{\bm{\Delta}})<\Phi({\bm{E}}_{k}) strictly, for the merit Φ \Phi of § 3.2 . On rejection λ ← 10 ​ λ \lambda\leftarrow 10\lambda and the same linear system is re-solved
with the new damping; the Jacobian is rebuilt only after an accepted
step. Up to 16 16 trials are allowed per step on the retrofitted hosts, and
four in the deployed configuration of § 4.3 . On acceptance λ ← max ⁡ ( λ / 2 , 10 − 6 ) \lambda\leftarrow\max(\lambda/2,10^{-6}) and is carried into the next
step rather than reset. The solve terminates when the mean squared residual Φ / m \Phi/m falls below 10 − 10 10^{-10} , the deployed configuration of
§ 4.3 using 10 − 5 10^{-5} in its place (Appendix H );
when a step exhausts its trials, when tr ⁡ ( 𝑱 ​ 𝑱 ⊤ ) \operatorname{tr}({\bm{J}}{\bm{J}}^{\top}) underflows, or at the step budget;
it returns the last accepted state. The m × m m\times m system is solved
by LU with partial pivoting in single precision with TF32 disabled;
a non-finite solution is treated as a rejected trial. What one accepted step costs. Building 𝑱 {\bm{J}} costs m m reverse-mode products through the frozen decoder; forming 𝑱 ​ 𝑱 ⊤ {\bm{J}}{\bm{J}}^{\top} costs O ⁡ ( m 2 ​ P ) O(m^{2}P) ; the solve costs O ⁡ ( m 3 ) O(m^{3}) ; recovering
the primal step costs O ⁡ ( m ​ P ) O(mP) . With m = 144 m=144 and P ∈ [ 10 4 , 10 5 ] P\in[10^{4},10^{5}] the decoder passes dominate. A rejected trial adds
one O ⁡ ( m 3 ) O(m^{3}) re-solve and nothing else. Reported quantities. Control error is the mean over
anchors of the Euclidean distance between the decoded joint and its
target, in metres; it is a different functional from the merit Φ \Phi . Relative state motion is ∥ 𝑬 R − 𝑬 0 ∥ 2 / ∥ 𝑬 0 ∥ 2 \lVert{\bm{E}}_{R}-{\bm{E}}_{0}\rVert_{2}/\lVert{\bm{E}}_{0}\rVert_{2} , a latent-space quantity. Steps-to-a-centimetre is the first accepted step at
which control error falls below 10 − 2 10^{-2} m. Scale normalisation. Replacing
equation 5 by the same absolute damping on
every host breaks the transfer: step-3 control error ( n = 32 n{=}32 ) rises
from 0.0435 0.0435 to 0.3920 0.3920 m on MoMask and from 0.0017 0.0017 to 0.0166 0.0166 m on MDM, while MotionLCM, whose Gram scale sits near unity,
is unchanged at 0.204 0.204 m. Gauss–Newton against first-order descent. The
same state, decoder, residual and clips admit any optimiser, so we
ran Adam on 1 2 ​ ∥ 𝒓 ∥ 2 \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert{\bm{r}}\rVert^{2} through the frozen decoder
alone, on MDM and MoMask (validation, n = 64 n{=}64 ), with the learning
rate set to η \eta times the standard deviation of the state, η ∈ { 0.01 , 0.03 , 0.1 } \eta\in\{0.01,0.03,0.1\} , 400 400 iterations, and the best η \eta chosen after the fact; timing covers the update only, as for the
solver, in a run separate from the timings of § 4.1 . On MDM, Adam stands at 0.041 0.041 m after 0.46 0.46 s and 0.016 0.016 m after 0.92 0.92 s, where the solver stands at 0.038 0.038 m
(two steps, 0.66 0.66 s) and 0.010 0.010 m (three, 0.99 0.99 s); at 1.3 1.3 s the solver is below 10 − 4 10^{-4} m at depth five and Adam is
at 0.006 0.006 m after 1.85 1.85 s. On MoMask, Adam is ahead early, 0.024 0.024 m at 0.79 0.79 s against the solver’s 0.131 0.131 m at two
steps, the two meet at a centimetre ( 0.011 0.011 m at 1.56 1.56 s against 0.011 0.011 m at depth five, 1.95 1.95 s), and below it the solver pulls
away, 0.0002 0.0002 m at depth sixteen ( 3.5 3.5 s) against 0.005 0.005 m
after 400 400 iterations ( 3.1 3.1 s). Mean contact-speed skating is the
same for both optimisers at matched error, 4.5 4.5 – 4.8 × 4.8\times on MDM
and 1.5 1.5 – 1.6 × 1.6\times on MoMask: the physical cost belongs to the
decoder, not to the optimiser. What the curvature buys is the last
order of magnitude, from the centimetre down, at equal wall-clock. Appendix B Choice of metric Replacing the identity by 𝚺 {\bm{\Sigma}} in equation 3 gives 𝚫 = − 𝚺 ​ 𝑱 ⊤ ​ ( 𝑱 ​ 𝚺 ​ 𝑱 ⊤ + μ ​ 𝑰 ) − 1 ​ 𝒓 {\bm{\Delta}}=-{\bm{\Sigma}}{\bm{J}}^{\top}({\bm{J}}{\bm{\Sigma}}{\bm{J}}^{\top}+\mu{\bm{I}})^{-1}{\bm{r}} . We
compared the identity against a diagonal state covariance and the full
codebook covariance on our own generator, sweeping solve depth on the
validation split (Table 4 ). Identity and diagonal track
each other at every depth on both axes. The codebook covariance reaches
the anchors more slowly and costs a factor of four in FID from the
first step onward, so we use the identity throughout. Depth zero is the untouched generation, and its FID of 0.171 0.171 is the
highest in the identity column: the first accepted step reduces FID to 0.090 0.090 while cutting control error by 46 % 46\% , and FID then stays below the
untouched value. Table 4: Solve depth against solver metric, on the post-hoc-trained

Appendix D Temporal basis of the update The update is confined to a temporal basis of width w w frames — the
increment for each state channel is the linear interpolation of ⌈ T / w ⌉ \lceil T/w\rceil knots placed w w frames apart, the first and last
on the first and last frame, so each knot carries a triangular bump of
support 2 ​ w 2w frames; the basis has rank C ​ ⌈ T / w ⌉ C\lceil T/w\rceil for C C channels, carries no normalisation, and at w = 1 w{=}1 is the identity, so
that arm is the unmodified solve. On the frame-local hosts w w is in
motion frames; on MoMask the basis lives on the token axis of its
stride-four tokeniser, so w w is in tokens, 4 ​ w 4w frames. Everything else is held: weights, frozen decoder,
clips, anchors, damping and accept schedule. Reading the intervention
against the temporal support the host’s own decoder already carries
gives the two directions in § 4.2 . Table 6: Intervention on a fixed host ( n = 128 n{=}128 ): the update

constraints against a state of 10 4 10^{4} – 10 5 10^{5} dimensions, which is
what makes the projection small. MotionLCM is the one host in this
study where that margin closes. Its sequence-VAE latent is 512 512 dimensions, and the six-point request at K = 8 K{=}8 fixes 144 144 of them
— 28 28 percent, against a state of tens of thousands of coordinates on every other host. The solve behaves as the disproportion predicts. It reaches 1 1 cm at
depth 40 40 , where CondMDI, MDM and our own generator reach it at

buys per step is simply smaller, and each Jacobian row costs a VAE
decode, so depth 40 40 takes 30.0 30.0 s of solve against a generation
that takes 0.015 0.015 s. The

Quality against the released control method. Table 7 scores three hosts under one evaluator, every row, generated and reference alike, decoded to joints and its 263 263 -d features re-extracted from them, so the evaluator sees only what the control moved: the host’s unconstrained sample, its released control method, and SCAMP at the first recorded depth that matches the released method’s anchor error, with the wall-clock of § 4.1 . The quality cost orders by decoder family as the physical cost of Table 2 does. On the windowed host SCAMP reaches half the released method’s anchor error in a fifth of its time at equal Top-3, paying FID 0.236 0.236 against 0.103 0.103 ; on the VAE host it matches the error at parity in time and pays more; on the frame-local analytic host the correction is the sharp limit of § 3.5 , and the quality goes with it. All hosts receive the same
clip list, the same anchor frames and the same targets. An automated
conformance gate verifies byte-level equality of the clip list and the
anchor tensor, together with solver parameters, damping constant, row
cap, and the TF32 and seeding state, before any host is measured; its
output ships with the code. Timing is per host on one card, and the released-budget DNO measurements were taken on an H100 and the
rest on one A100. Clips are generated one at a time ( n = 64 n{=}64 ), and the sweep is one solve of sixteen accepted steps read at the depths of Table 1 (MotionLCM’s continues to depth 48 48 , Appendix E ); the times of § 4.1 are generation plus the solve up to the depth that matches the incumbent (MDM three, MaskControl five, OmniControl two, CondMDI one, MotionLCM eight; MoMask and MARDM to a centimetre, five), read from the same runs. Generation runs each host’s released sampler: MDM at 100 100 DDIM steps; OmniControl and CondMDI with their 1000 1000 -step samplers, OmniControl at its fixed 196 196 frames; MoMask and MaskControl’s branch at 10 10 masked steps, MaskControl’s own method adding 100 100 token-optimisation iterations per step and 600 600 at the end; MARDM at 18 18 ; MotionLCM at one. The starting states are the hosts’ text-conditioned samples with their control machinery off: OmniControl without its spatial guidance, CondMDI’s unconditional checkpoint, MotionLCM before its latent optimisation; MaskControl’s sweep starts from its trained control branch’s output with the token optimisation switched off, since that branch is the model. Noise floor. Twenty repetitions of the deployed configuration give 95 95 percent intervals of ± 0.0036 \pm 0.0036 in FID, ± 7 × 10 − 4 \pm 7\times 10^{-4} m in control error, ± 4 × 10 − 4 \pm 4\times 10^{-4} in foot skating and below 10 − 4 10^{-4} in jerk. On the retrofitted hosts, one configuration run twice on one card ( n = 8 n{=}8 , identical seed) gives a spread in control error of 1.8 × 10 − 4 1.8\times 10^{-4} m
averaged over the depth grid, 1.2 × 10 − 3 1.2\times 10^{-3} m at depth three
where the solve is mid-descent and the accept–retry schedule can take
a different branch, and 9 × 10 − 5 9\times 10^{-5} m from depth eight onwards,
where the residual is small and the step is essentially determined. Metric conventions. Foot skating is computed on the clip
truncated to its true length. Every skating number in this paper is computed under the truncated
convention on one evaluation stack. What the backward pass carries. The solve enters the graph
through the straight-through surrogate of equation 9 . Gradient
flows through the last few sampler states and the differentiable
suffix. Endpoint samples and suffix transitions are hard on the
forward pass; the discrete row selection of the next generator and the
truncated support of the guided posterior are held fixed in the
backward pass; the sampled prefix carries no graph. Appendix G Proofs G.1 Proposition 1 Fix an endpoint y y , write δ k = δ ⁡ ( k , y ) \delta_{k}=\delta(k,y) and δ ¯ t = ∑ i q t ​ ( i ∣ y ) ​ δ i \bar{\delta}_{t}=\sum_{i}q_{t}(i\mid y)\delta_{i} . Differentiating

clean state; the controlled output is the decode of the corrected
continuous state, which is never re-quantised. 1: text c c , anchors 𝒜 \mathcal{A} , grid t 0 < ⋯ < t N − 1 t_{0}<\dots<t_{N-1} ,

posterior at ( 𝑿 n , c , 𝒜 ) ({\bm{X}}_{n},c,\mathcal{A}) 5: 𝑿 n + 1 ← {\bm{X}}_{n+1}\leftarrow first event under rates sampled from π n \pi_{n} ⊳ \triangleright equations 7 and 8 6: end for 7: π N − 1 ← \pi_{N-1}\leftarrow posterior at ( 𝑿 N − 1 , c , 𝒜 ) ({\bm{X}}_{N-1},c,\mathcal{A}) ; 𝑿 N ∼ π N − 1 {\bm{X}}_{N}\sim\pi_{N-1} 8: 𝑬 0 ← 𝑪 ⁡ [ 𝑿 N ] {\bm{E}}_{0}\leftarrow{\bm{C}}[{\bm{X}}_{N}] ⊳ \triangleright hard clean code embedding 9: 𝑬 ^ ← GN ⁡ ( 𝑬 0 , 𝒜 ) \hat{\bm{E}}\leftarrow\operatorname{GN}({\bm{E}}_{0};\mathcal{A}) , R R accepted steps ⊳ \triangleright equation 4 , identity metric 10: return 𝒟 ⁡ ( 𝑬 ^ ) \mathcal{D}(\hat{\bm{E}}) ⊳ \triangleright decode the corrected state directly Solver-coupled versus post-hoc training. Both arms
are measured from the state their sampler emits before any solve,
under the shared solver of Table 1 (validation, n = 1024 n{=}1024 ). The solver-coupled sampler emits 0.314 0.314 m against 0.367 0.367 m from the same model trained post hoc, whose sampler
carries no solver. Two accepted steps take them to 0.083 0.083 m, the deployed output,
and to 0.107 0.107 m; a centimetre takes 4.36 4.36 accepted
steps against 4.56 4.56 , moving the state 0.338 0.338 against 0.359 0.359 in
relative norm. Mean contact speed runs 0.165 0.165 against 0.183 0.183 m/s
at the emitted state and 0.201 0.201 against 0.220 0.220 after two steps.
Training through the solve lowers the emitted error from 0.367 0.367 to 0.314 0.314 m and keeps that margin along the solve. Stage 1 trains the text-conditioned prior: sample t ∼ 𝒰 ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) t\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1) , corrupt the clean token sequence with q t ( ⋅ ∣ z ⋆ ) q_{t}(\cdot\mid z^{\star}) from equation 6 , and train the
transformer to predict z ⋆ z^{\star} with cross-entropy, dropping the text
condition with a fixed probability so that the same network supplies
the unconditional branch used by classifier-free guidance. Stage 2
adds the anchor conditioning of § 3.6 and fine-tunes the
full model, still with cross-entropy alone, over a ladder of anchor
densities in which the first and last frames are always observed.
Stage 3 is the on-policy calibration. The model generates with its own sampler; anchor conditioning switches on at step 10 10 of the 20 20 , the last four transitions retain gradients, and the terminal solve runs on the final state inside the graph through equation 9 at R = 2 R{=}2 accepted steps, λ 0 = 10 − 2 \lambda_{0}{=}10^{-2} , four trials, a tolerance of 10 − 5 10^{-5} on the mean squared residual and the 48 48 -anchor row cap of the deployed configuration. The objective is ℒ = ℒ CE + 0.1 ​ ℒ local , ℒ local = ∥ 𝒟 ⁡ ( 𝑬 ST ) − 𝒀 ∥ ¯ 𝒜 + 0.25 ​ ∥ 𝒟 ⁡ ( 𝑬 ST ) − 𝒀 ∥ ¯ ℋ , \mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}+0.1\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{local}},\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{local}}=\overline{\lVert\mathcal{D}({\bm{E}}_{\mathrm{ST}})-{\bm{Y}}\rVert}_{\mathcal{A}}+0.25\,\overline{\lVert\mathcal{D}({\bm{E}}_{\mathrm{ST}})-{\bm{Y}}\rVert}_{\mathcal{H}}, (13) with ℒ CE \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}} the rollout cross-entropy on the sampler’s own logits, and ℒ local \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{local}} the mean Euclidean joint error of the straight-through decode against the reference clip, averaged over the anchored frame–joint pairs 𝒜 \mathcal{A} and over the halo ℋ \mathcal{H} of frames within two of an anchor. The solved state enters the objective through 𝒟 ⁡ ( 𝑬 ST ) \mathcal{D}({\bm{E}}_{\mathrm{ST}}) , whose forward value is the corrected state and whose gradient reaches the differentiable posterior state of equation 9 . Stage 3 is short: the deployed checkpoint is taken at epoch 25 25 . The
path constants of § 3.6 are p = 2 p{=}2 , α = 0.9 \alpha{=}0.9 and c β = 3.0 c_{\beta}{=}3.0 , with N = 20 N{=}20 sampler steps on a uniform grid over [ 0.1 , 0.9 ] [0.1,0.9] , the tokens drawn uniformly at random at its first point, so β ˙ \dot{\beta} is evaluated away from both endpoints of the path, guidance scale 4.0 4.0 and top- k k truncation to the highest-scoring tenth of the codebook. Sizes. The masked transformer is 8 8 layers of width 384 384 with 6 6 heads and a 1536 1536 -wide feed-forward block, dropout 0.2 0.2 , and a conditioning drop probability of 0.1 0.1 for
classifier-free guidance. The frozen tokeniser is a single quantiser
over 512 512 codes of dimension 512 512 ; its convolutional decoder is 512 512 wide and 3 3 deep with dilation growth 3 3 , and runs at unit temporal stride, neither downsampling nor upsampling in time. The residual encoder reads 54 54 control
features per frame and injects through rank- 64 64 adapters. Clips run
to 196 196 frames. Training uses batch 48 48 at learning rate 5 × 10 − 5 5{\times}10^{-5} , stepped by 0.1 0.1 at 70 70 , 80 80 and 90 90 percent of
the schedule. References Amos and Kolter (2017) B. Amos and J. Z. Kolter OptNet: differentiable optimization as a layer in neural networks . In Proceedings of the 34th International Conference on Machine Learning,
